[b]March 11, 2028: We are allied to idiots[/b]
Gentlemen, why are we together again? Asked Cahit Alparslan as the three men and a small group of aides sat once again in the conference room they had been in not twenty four hours earlier.
The war has escalated, replied the Shah bluntly, Wuloosyan allies attempted and allegedly successfully completed a decap strike against Rosenmarkke,
Cahit frowned, his jowls beginning to tremble, Edis put his face into his hands and declared, Sir, we are allied to idiots! He gave a laugh-sob.
Your honour, intoned Cahit with deep solemnity, It is in times like these where our nation must reconsider its position on the world stage, and the optics of such a position, may I ask a question of this? Asked Cahit.
The Shah inclined his head in approval.
Cahit leaned back in his motorchair, the seat giving an ominous creak, Would it be good to remind our allies that there are those nationswho are not friendly to themwho are willing to not abide by the rules of the international nuclear treaties?
I do not find reminding our friends, who are also nuclear capable of nuclear matters, I do not find that effective messaging, replied the shah.
Cahit nodded, Would it be prudent to send them a box of jam? 
Edis sobbed, the shah blinked, Jam? He asked, You want to send them a gift basket? 
A message my dear shah, replied Cahit tapping the table, A message warning Julian of his fragile humanity, 
Wouldnt that seem like we support Rosenmarkke? Asked Edis.
Which we dont, interjected the shah.
Ah, tsk tsk, intoned Cahit spreading his hands out, No no no, we would be merely warning them that their nation, and its actions, will reverberate around the world, he said drawing a circle in the air with his pointer finger, Glory. To. Yzakastan. He intoned, chortling.
We will maintain our current stance, condemn the unnecessary violence and call for peaceful resolution, replied the shah, Meeting dismissed,

[i][b]F R É T H U N E ─[/b][/i] On the night of March 25, a wave of riots and mass protests erupted in the city of [b]Fréthune[/b], [b]Baria Region[/b], on the island of [b]Épiroux[/b]. The unrest broke out shortly after the [b]Pirn Parliament[/b] abolished the legal right of humans to participate in politics and serve in the legislature. Like a ticking time bomb finally detonating, thousands of people flooded into the streets at 11:40 p.m. local time.

Enraged demonstrators hurled Molotov cocktails while others smashed vehicles, bringing the citys traffic to a complete standstill. Despite rapid deployment, regional police were unable to regain control. The situation escalated rapidly as several police stations were overrun by agitators, who seized weapons from inside. What began as a riot and protest quickly evolved into an armed uprising, forcing the government to immediately replace the local administration and deploy large numbers of anti-riot units from multiple regions to restore order.

According to on-site correspondents in Fréthune, anti-riot forces resorted to tear gas and high-pressure water cannons to push back the crowd while forming shield walls. However, this tactic collapsed when gunshots were fired from within the demonstrators. Riot-control units subsequently shifted to the use of firearms to neutralize armed protesters while attempting to safeguard unarmed civilians. Even so, multiple reports indicate that many protesters were killed, either by stray bullets from riot police or by armed demonstrators themselves.

The scale of the violence was so severe that the government deployed the regular military, the [b]Pirn Defence Force (PDF)[/b], to suppress the unrest. Power and internet services were cut across the city, plunging non-participants into panic. Many residents reportedly fled into nearby suburban towns during the night.

The riot lasted five hours before authorities regained control. Official statistics report [i]1,000 deaths[/i], including police and riot-control personnel, [i]934 injuries[/i], and more than half of the citys population directly affected. Fréthune later imposed a strict curfew, banned gatherings of more than three people, and ordered continuous police patrols. The PDF subsequently withdrew after completing its mission.

As of now, the city remains under curfew. Many residents have yet to return, some suffering from psychological trauma, while others have been left homeless after the destruction caused by rioters. The event, now officially referred to as [i][b]The Sunday Riot[/b][/i], is considered one of the largest recorded uprisings in Pirns history. It has also prompted the government to re-evaluate human participation in politics alongside furry citizens.
